---
title: "Seasonality and autocorrelation"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r library}
library(lagprotest)
```

The permutation schemes of `lagged_protest()` keep the autocorrelation of
`Y` under the null, but each rests on assumptions about the seasonal cycle
and the noise around it (see
[Choosing a permutation scheme](permutation-schemes.html)). Two features of
real series break those assumptions: a seasonal cycle that both series
share and that is not close to a sine wave, and strong autocorrelation of
the anomalies around the cycle. This article describes the two
preprocessing options that address them, `deseason` and `prewhiten`, and
when to use each.

## What each option does

Both options are applied to `X` and `Y` after they are truncated to whole
cycles (`period`) and before their columns are standardized (`scale`):

* `deseason = "monthly"` subtracts from every column the mean of each
  position in the cycle, for example the mean of all Januaries, of all
  Februaries, and so on. It needs `period` and at least two whole cycles,
  and takes the first row as position 1 of the cycle.
* `prewhiten = "prais"` replaces every column by its residuals from an
  AR(1) process, using the Prais–Winsten transformation, which keeps all
  rows. The AR(1) coefficient of each column is its lag-1 autocorrelation
  after any `deseason`, and is returned in `fit$rho`.

## Removing a shared seasonal cycle

Two independent series that share a seasonal cycle are concordant at every
lag, because Procrustes analysis compares the shapes of the two
trajectories and their cycles have the same shape. Phase surrogates handle
a shared sinusoidal cycle, because a sine wave keeps its shape when its
phase changes, but not an abrupt one: a sawtooth or a short pulse is abrupt
only because the phases of its harmonics are aligned, and the surrogates
draw new phases for every harmonic.

The simulation below generates two independent series with the same
sawtooth cycle over four years of monthly data:

```{r sawtooth-null}
null <- simulate_lagged_series(n_times = 48, waveform = "sawtooth",
                               noise_sd = 0.5, seed = 1)
fit_raw <- lagged_protest(null$X, null$Y, lags = 0:4, period = 12,
                          seed = 1)
fit_des <- lagged_protest(null$X, null$Y, lags = 0:4, period = 12,
                          deseason = "monthly", seed = 1)
c(raw = fit_raw$p.global, deseasoned = fit_des$p.global)
```

Without preprocessing, the test rejects the null for this pair of
independent series; with the seasonal means removed, it does not. This is
not a rare pair: the test without preprocessing rejected for 9 of the first
20 seeds. Over many such pairs, it rejected the null in about a third of
the replicates at α = 0.05 (see
[Simulating lagged series](simulating-series.html#seasonal-waveforms)),
whereas with `deseason = "monthly"` it rejected at about the nominal rate
for every waveform tested.

Removing the seasonal means changes the question. Without it, the test asks
whether the two trajectories are concordant at some lag, seasonal cycle
included; with it, whether their departures from the average cycle are. The
second question is the one that a shared response to the calendar cannot
answer, and is the safer one whenever both series are seasonal. A lag in
the seasonal cycle itself, as when a response peaks two months after its
driver every year, is removed together with the cycle: it can be described
by comparing the seasonal means, but it is not tested.

## Removing autocorrelation of the anomalies

Phase surrogates keep the autocorrelation of `Y`, but in short series with
strongly autocorrelated noise the test was still liberal in simulations
(see [Choosing a permutation scheme](permutation-schemes.html)). Prais–Winsten
prewhitening removes that autocorrelation before the test. Ordinary
prewhitening, which drops the first row, should not be applied by hand
after removing seasonal means: the dropped row breaks the balance of the
cycle positions and made the test strongly liberal in simulations.

The residual autocorrelation reported by `lagged_protest()` helps decide.
The series below have strongly autocorrelated noise and no seasonality:

```{r ar-null}
ar <- simulate_lagged_series(n_times = 24, amplitude = 0, autocorr = 0.9,
                             seed = 3)
fit <- lagged_protest(ar$X, ar$Y, lags = 0:4, seed = 1)
fit$ar1
fit_pw <- lagged_protest(ar$X, ar$Y, lags = 0:4, prewhiten = "prais",
                         seed = 1)
round(fit_pw$rho$X, 2)
fit_pw$ar1
```

For non-seasonal series with an AR(1) coefficient of 0.9, the Type I error
of the phase scheme was 0.19 with 24 samples and 0.10 with 48, and 0.03 to
0.04 after prewhitening (400 replicates, 199 surrogates).

Prewhitening has a cost when it is combined with `deseason`: when an abrupt
seasonal cycle varies in amplitude from year to year and the noise is
strongly autocorrelated, the test was liberal (about 0.10 for a sawtooth with AR(1) of 0.9),
whereas `deseason` alone stayed close to the nominal level. Requesting
`prewhiten` for a seasonal series without `deseason` triggers a warning,
because prewhitening does not remove a shared cycle and made the test more
liberal in simulations of series with several abrupt cycles.

## A recommended sequence

1. Plot both series and decide whether a seasonal cycle is present and how
   long it is.
2. If the series span several whole cycles, give `period`, so that both are
   truncated to whole cycles, and use `deseason = "monthly"` unless the
   seasonal cycle itself is what you want to test.
3. If they span a single cycle, seasonal means cannot be removed. Phase
   surrogates then assume that any shared cycle is close to sinusoidal;
   check whether the seasonal trajectories are smooth, and interpret
   concordance with that limitation in mind.
4. Look at the residual autocorrelation in `fit$ar1`. It is biased
   downwards in short series (about 0.4 for a true AR(1) coefficient of 0.9
   with 24 samples, in the example above), so a clearly positive value in a
   short series may hide strong autocorrelation. In that case, consider
   `prewhiten = "prais"`, and report results with and without it if the
   seasonal cycle is abrupt.
5. Report the preprocessing used, which `print()` shows, together with the
   global p-value for the scan.

With simulated data matching your design, the
[Simulating lagged series](simulating-series.html) article shows how to
check calibration and power of each combination before analyzing real
data.
